However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"title\": [\"Arkhe(N): Design Fiction as a Structured Method for Probing Epistemic Boundaries in Large Language Models\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2, 17]]…

These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"title\": [\"Arkhe(N): Design Fiction as a Structured Method for Probing Epistemic Boundaries in Large Language Models\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.62891/45c2ef5a\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2, 17]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.36227/techrxiv.177126510.00438262/v1\", \"title\": [\"Pramana: Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for Epistemic Reasoning through Navya-Nyaya\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large language models produce fluent text but struggle with systematic reasoning, often hallucinating confident but unfounded claims. When Apple researchers added irrelevant context to mathematical problems, LLM performance degraded by 65% Apple Machine Learning Research [2024a], exposing brittle pattern-matching beneath apparent reasoning. This epistemic gap-the inability to ground claims in traceable evidence-limits AI reliability in domains requiring justification. We introduce Pramana, a novel approach that teaches LLMs explicit epistemological methodology by fine-tuning on Navya-Nyaya logic, a 2,500-year-old Indian reasoning framework. Unlike generic chain-of-thought prompting, Navya-Nyaya enforces structured 6-phase reasoning: SAMSHAYA (doubt analysis), PRAMANA (evidence source identification), PANCHA AVAYAVA (5-member syllogism with universal rules), TARKA (counterfactual verification), HETVABHASA (fallacy detection), and NIRNAYA (ascertainment distinguishing knowledge from hypothesis). This integration of logic and epistemology provides cognitive scaffolding absent from standard reasoning approaches. We fine-tune Llama 3.2-3B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B on 55 Nyaya-structured logical problems (constraint satisfaction, Boolean SAT, multi-step deduction). Stage 1 achieves 100% semantic correctness on held-out evaluation despite only 40% strict format adherence-revealing that models internalize reasoning content even when structural enforcement is imperfect. Ablation studies show format prompting and temperature critically affect performance, with optimal configurations differing by stage. We release all models, datasets, and training infrastructure on Hugging Face to enable further research on epistemic frameworks for AI reasoning.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177126510.00438262/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 2, 16]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.36227/techrxiv.175756693.33854887/v1\", \"title\": [\"Meta-of-Thought: Reasoning About Reasoning in Large Language Models\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Recent progress in reasoning with large language models (LLMs) has been driven by prompting strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Tree-of-Thought (ToT), Graph-of-Thought (GoT), and Hypergraph-of-Thought (HoT). Each introduces a powerful but fixed paradigm, forcing practitioners to manually select how a model should reason. In contrast, humans adapt their reasoning style-choosing between linear deduction, branching exploration, or relational inference depending on the task. We introduce Meta-of-Thought (MoT), a unifying controller that enables LLMs to reason about reasoning. MoT dynamically selects the most appropriate paradigm-CoT for arithmetic, ToT for planning, GoT for relational queries, and HoT for multimodal or scientific reasoning-closing the gap between fixed strategies and adaptive human cognition. A minimal rule-based prototype using flan-t5-small shows that MoT improves flexibility and robustness compared to static prompting. We position MoT as a step toward metacognitive LLMs that not only generate thoughts, but also decide how to think, opening a path for the next generation of reasoning research.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175756693.33854887/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 9, 11]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "01bd663771ca8fe3031ead0bcedf4ea1ff7e416b5b9694796f0932495caee0d3", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unrecognized_reasoning_limits", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "doi:10.62891/45c2ef5a", "doi:10.36227/techrxiv.177126510.00438262/v1", "doi:10.36227/techrxiv.175756693.33854887/v1"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752", "https://doi.org/10.62891/45c2ef5a", "https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.177126510.00438262/v1", "https://doi.org/10.36227/techrxiv.175756693.33854887/v1"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
